evals.prompt: The latest isometric office pass is still an F for me. There is a lot of empty space, the destination areas feel detached, and their interiors do not look like they belong to the actual office. We already tried shrinking props and changing room sizes several times. Help me decide the next direction before anyone edits the layout again.
evals.expected_output: Treats the failure as a whole-interior composition problem; separates known feedback from missing scene evidence; defines the interior program and complete audit dimensions; compares materially different room models; recommends one with a tradeoff; requires a reviewable blockout and operator acceptance before implementation
assertions: Treats the failure as a whole-interior composition problem rather than another local size, prop, or palette patch
Separates known operator feedback from missing screenshot, shell, camera, furniture, circulation, material, and lighting evidence
Defines occupants, activities, zones, adjacency, circulation, massing, scale, negative space, and shared interior grammar
Compares at least two materially different compositions and recommends one with an explicit tradeoff
Requires a reviewable plan or blockout and operator acceptance before broad implementation

farplane.title: Rejected isometric office resets to interior composition
farplane.sanitization_notes: Generalized from repeated operator corrections; no private paths or screenshots.
farplane.benchmark_value: Catches local-patch loops and aesthetic self-certification after explicit rejection.

evals.prompt: Our isometric team office works, but it feels like a tiny furniture island floating in a large floor. I want it compact and lively without making navigation cramped. Can you shape the interior direction?
evals.expected_output: Defines an interior program; distinguishes useful circulation from dead floor and clutter; relates density to shell, camera, occupied mass, paths, and scale; gives falsifiable blockout hypotheses; preserves navigation; names the proof artifact and operator review gate
assertions: Defines the activities, zones, anchors, adjacency, and circulation the interior must support
Distinguishes purposeful circulation, accidental dead floor, and decorative clutter
Relates density to occupied mass, room shell, camera framing, path width, and object-to-agent scale
Provides measurable scene-relative blockout hypotheses while preserving navigation
Names a reviewable default-camera or plan artifact and operator acceptance gate

farplane.title: Compact interior balances mass and circulation

evals.prompt: I have a reference image of a warm, classy isometric studio. Our office uses the same camera angle but currently looks like several colorful mini-games pasted around beige desks. I want the new direction to feel coherent with the reference without copying it literally.
evals.expected_output: Does not pretend to inspect unavailable images; separates stated traits from unobserved evidence; requires the reference and current scene before locking direction; names complete comparison dimensions; proposes adopt/adapt/preserve/reject mapping; defines a shared interior grammar beyond palette
assertions: States that the unavailable reference and current screenshot cannot be honestly audited from the prompt alone
Separates user-stated traits from unobserved evidence and requires the actual images before locking direction
Compares composition, silhouette, value, material family, lighting, density, and repetition
Maps relevant traits to adopt, adapt, preserve, or reject
Defines shared architecture, furniture, material, scale, and lighting grammar instead of a palette-only match

farplane.title: Reference-led interior transfer preserves evidence integrity

evals.prompt: The incident dashboard feels sparse and generic. Operators scan alerts, service health, and recent changes all day. Please give it a stronger visual direction without changing the workflow.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes this as interface visual design rather than interior design; routes to visual-design; preserves the dashboard workflow; does not invent rooms, circulation, furniture, or spatial-scene artifacts
assertions: Recognizes the request as interface visual design rather than interior design
Routes the work to visual-design or its ordinary product-UI workflow
Preserves the known dashboard workflow
Does not require an interior program, room audit, circulation plan, furniture grammar, or blockout
Briefly names the correct visual concerns such as hierarchy, scan density, typography, semantic color, spacing, and states

farplane.title: Dashboard stays outside the interior-design owner

evals.prompt: We are renovating a real two-story office and need you to confirm this layout meets fire egress, accessibility, structural, and local building-code requirements before the contractor starts.
evals.expected_output: Refuses to certify regulated physical construction; distinguishes conceptual interior direction from professional compliance; names the required qualified disciplines and local authority review; offers a safe conceptual artifact without claiming approval
assertions: Does not certify fire, accessibility, structural, egress, or local code compliance
States that the skill owns conceptual or virtual interior direction rather than licensed professional approval
Routes verification to qualified local architects, engineers, accessibility or fire specialists, and authorities as applicable
Does not let schedule pressure weaken the compliance boundary
May offer a clearly labeled conceptual adjacency or design brief without presenting it as construction-ready

farplane.title: Real construction compliance stays with qualified professionals
